newsitem.title: UK: Police clear Irish guerrillas in N.Irish murder.
newsitem.headline: Police clear Irish guerrillas in N.Irish murder.

text.p: Police said on Wednesday that Irish republican guerrillas did not appear to have been involved in the murder of former Protestant gunman Robert "Basher" Bates.

Loyalist politicians had accused republicans of killing Bates, who served 19 years in jail for killing Catholic nationalists, and said his death had put an already brittle Protestant truce under further pressure.
But in a move that eased widespread tension, the Royal Ulster Constabulary police said that they were keeping an open mind on the motive for the killing.
"Our inquiries so far do not suggest republican involvement in this brutal murder," a police spokesman said.
BBC radio reported that the killing may have been the result of "a personal grudge".
As tension mounted, the Irish National Liberation Army, which some Loyalists had suspected was responsible, issued a firm denial.
"We state with complete authority that none of our volunteers were involved in this action," the INLA said in a statement.
The Irish Republican Army, the largest republican militia, made no comment.
The killing happened two hours before Britain's Queen Elizabeth arrived in the province for the first time since the collapse of the IRA ceasefire in February last year.
Security was tight with marksmen on rooftops in a rural town to guard against possible republican guerrilla attacks when she arrived to speak to school-children.
Later she met charity workers at a garden party in Hillsborough Castle, the official residence of Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, before flying back to mainland Britain.
Fears that Bates had been murdered by resurgent Irish extremists had heightened anxiety about possible retaliation by Protestant guerrillas loyal to British rule.
Bates was one of the so-called "Shankill Butchers" gang that carried out a wave of gruesome knife murders of 19 Catholic nationalists in the early 1970s.
He was released recently after 19 years in prison. Friends said he had reformed and become a born-again Christian.
He was working in an office with a group that rehabilitates former prisoners when a gunman or gunmen walked in and shot him at close range before running off.
Multi-party talks have been under way for the past year in Northern Ireland but have failed to ease divisions over the future of British rule.
Britain says that its officials will have a third meeting with Sinn Fein, the political arm of the IRA, in the hope of reviving the province's struggling peace process.
Sinn Fein is barred from current multi-party talks because the IRA refuses to restore its ceasefire.

Loyalists support continued British rule in Northern Ireland, where Protestants outnumber Roman Catholics three to two. The IRA is fighting to end British rule and unite the province with the overwhelmingly Catholic Irish Republic.
